name: Representative democracy
summary: Representative democracy is government in which citizens choose officials by election to make laws and run the state for them, rather than deciding directly. Its defenders, from Madison to Mill, hold that delegation filters opinion, guards against majority faction and lets large societies govern themselves while remaining answerable to voters. It prescribes a form of rule, not an economic or cultural programme.
scope: The liberal-constitutional mainstream, based on Madison's Federalist No. 10 and Mill's Considerations on Representative Government, as summarised in the Wikipedia and Stanford entries. Excludes direct, participatory, soviet and corporatist alternatives. Most social and economic statements are left to party competition, so many answers are neutral or low-confidence.

sources.usedFor: Defining reference on representation; names Madison as the thinker most associated with a representative government of elected delegates.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Madison cites the absolute prohibition of titles of nobility as proof of the republican character of the system.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Madison says the representatives alone can propose and may refuse the supplies, calling the power of the purse their most complete and effectual weapon.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Madison holds it essential to a republic that government derives from the great body of the people, appointed directly or indirectly by them.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Madison states that the aim of the republic is to secure the public good and private rights against a majority faction while keeping popular government.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Mill names class legislation, government for the benefit of the dominant class, as one of the greatest dangers of democracy and seeks securities against it.

direct-votes.rationale: Madison holds that a pure democracy has no cure for faction and prefers delegation to elected representatives, and Mill argues that since all cannot take part personally the ideal type of government is representative.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: Mill devotes a chapter to the social conditions under which representative government is inapplicable, holding some peoples unfit for it.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Madison states that a dependence on the people is the primary control on government, with institutional precautions as auxiliaries.

experts-over-public.rationale: Mill would give a small expert commission the task of making laws and would give the educated plural votes, while keeping the assembly in control.

generational-constitutional-review.rationale: Madison objects to frequent appeals to the people to revise the constitution, because each would imply a defect in the government and weaken the veneration that stability needs.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: Madison says the tribunal that decides disputes over the boundary between federal and state jurisdiction must be established under the general government, as essential to prevent an appeal to the sword.

minority-veto.rationale: Madison relies on the majority defeating a minority faction by regular vote, rejecting a veto for the minority.

national-self-determination.rationale: Mill holds it a necessary condition of free institutions that the boundaries of governments coincide in the main with those of nationalities, while allowing exceptions where nationalities are intermingled.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Madison calls the elective mode of obtaining rulers the characteristic policy of republican government.

one-party-rule.rationale: Mill says it is an essential part of democracy that minorities be adequately represented and that without it there is only a false show of democracy.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Mill makes the assembly the ultimate controlling power over the government, while Madison warns that the legislature tends to engulf the other departments.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Mill holds that any participation, even in the smallest public function, is useful, while both he and Madison leave lawmaking to elected representatives.

property-franchise.rationale: Madison says the federal electors are not the rich more than the poor, and Mill requires literacy rather than property and calls property-based plural votes objectionable.

property-fundamental.rationale: Madison calls the protection of the different and unequal faculties of acquiring property the first object of government and treats a rage for an equal division of property as a wicked project.

proportional-representation.rationale: Mill presents proportional representation of minorities as essential to real democracy and backs Hare's scheme; Madison does not address the electoral formula.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Mill states the general principle that government boundaries should coincide in the main with nationalities, which favours uniting a divided nation, with exceptions for geographic or practical hindrances.

second-chamber.rationale: Madison defends a well-constructed Senate as necessary, and Mill judges two chambers desirable, so that neither holds undivided power, though he calls the question of modest weight.

separated-powers.rationale: Madison requires the departments of government to hold the means to resist one another ("Ambition must be made to counteract ambition"), and warns that the legislature tends to draw all power into itself.

single-common-good.rationale: Madison wants representatives who discern the true interest of the country, yet calls the regulation of interfering interests the principal task of modern legislation.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Madison counts it a strong bond between rulers and people that the representatives can make no law that does not operate fully on themselves as well.

state-harmful.rationale: Madison calls government the greatest reflection on human nature yet necessary ("If men were angels, no government would be necessary"), and names justice as the end of government.

strong-leader.rationale: Madison builds checks and divided power to slow concentrated power, and Mill makes the assembly the controller of the executive rather than the executive a master of it.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Madison rejects abolishing liberty to remove faction, calling that remedy worse than the disease, and expects a minority faction to be beaten by regular vote.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Mill holds that any participation in public functions is useful and that a people lacking public spirit cannot keep free government.

women-suffrage.rationale: Mill argues that sex is as irrelevant to a voice in government as height or hair colour and that women need it at least as much as men; Madison does not address it.

workers-councils.rationale: Mill treats an assembly chosen by all citizens as the centre of representative government and warns against class legislation by any one class.

missingStatements.text: Legislators should use their own judgment on behalf of voters rather than follow their instructions.
missingStatements.rationale: Burke's trustee model is the classic representative-democratic view, and Madison expects elected citizens to refine public opinion.

missingStatements.text: A legislature, not the executive, should hold the ultimate power to watch and control the government.
missingStatements.rationale: Mill says the proper office of a representative assembly is to watch and control the government.

missingStatements.text: Minorities should be given adequate representation in the legislature, not only the majority.
missingStatements.rationale: Mill states that adequate representation of minorities is an essential part of democracy.
missingStatements.declined: Near-universally endorsed in principle; proportional-representation covers the contested mechanism.

notes: Re-audited under rules 6 from Madison's Federalist papers (Nos. 10, 39, 48, 49, 51, 52, 57, 58, 63), Mill's Considerations on Representative Government and the Stanford Encyclopedia entries on democracy and political representation, all saved locally. Representative democracy prescribes a form of rule (elected delegates, checks on majorities), so only positions those texts state or that contradict them are answered; the earlier economic, social and foreign-policy answers rested on Wikipedia or on silence and are now null. Themes searched: nationality and federalism (Mill Chapters 16 and 17, Federalist 39), religion and race (Federalist 10 and 51, the Stanford entries, which state no position), economy and property, foreign policy and empire (Mill Chapter 18), elections and the franchise, executive and legislature, separation of powers, second chambers, minorities and faction, constitutional change, mandates and recall, civil liberties. The economy, society, culture, ecology, technology and world themes are not addressed by these sources and stay null. Mill's and Madison's views differ on legislative supremacy and the electoral formula, and the Federalist papers address the US constitution, so some answers are medium. Britannica could not be opened. Failing the uncertainty rule is the honest result.
